edits.value_json: "工 is a whole-graph pictograph proposed to depict a tool, though its precise object is disputed. Today it means work or labor; early records also use it for occupations, but the evidence does not establish a clear sequence linking these meanings."

"Pictographic: early forms are interpreted as a tool, with proposals including a carpenter’s square, but the precise object is disputed. 工 is treated as one pictured graph, not a combination of internal parts. A separate transmitted historical account glosses it as 巧飾, skilled finishing, and explains the shape as a person possessing 規榘; this is a distinct interpretation, not confirmation of a particular tool."
"工 is treated as one complete pictorial graph, proposed to depict a tool. Its exact referent is disputed; no separate internal components are identified."

"Labeled oracle-script and small-seal renderings show historical forms of 工. Early graphs are interpreted as tools, but the proposed object remains disputed. A separate account proposes that lower strokes changed from thicker forms to a thin horizontal; that graphic account does not settle the pictured object."

"The graph is interpreted as picturing a tool, with proposals including a carpenter’s square. The precise object remains disputed, and the cited accounts do not date the relevant artifacts. This is a proposal about the pictured graph, not an independently established word use or earliest attestation."

"Reported oracle-bone examples use 工 for status or occupation, including craft-related uses. A bronze inscription is reported to use it in an official title interpreted as 司空. Keep title/status and craft-worker uses distinct; their relationship is unresolved."

"工 is used for a craft worker or skilled maker, as in 百工 and the received Zhouli tradition. Contemporary dictionary examples also list worker uses such as 木工 and 矿工. These attestations support the use but do not date its beginning or establish its relation to the proposed tool interpretation."
"工 currently means work or labor. The evidence does not give a dated sequence showing how this use developed from the proposed tool or craft-worker senses."

"In cited bronze-inscription and Warring States-slip contexts, 工 is read as 功, ‘achievement’. This is graphic interchange or borrowing in those contexts, not proof that 工’s work sense developed into achievement."

"The cited artifact examples are not individually dated in these accounts, so they do not establish the earliest attestation of each use. Glosses and listed meanings alone do not demonstrate a chronological semantic chain."

"工 is a whole-graph picture proposed to show a tool, though the exact object is disputed. Today it means work or labor; it is also used for craft workers, but the evidence does not establish a clear sequence linking these meanings."
"Read 工 as one complete picture, proposed to show a tool. The exact object is disputed; no separate internal parts are identified."
